assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work changed how economists and policymakers understand the labour-market effects of technology and import competition. It combines the task-based view of technological change, the skill-demand and wage-structure literature, and the local labour-market estimates of the China trade shock. Its influence reaches well beyond labour economics into trade, political economy and the debate on AI. The empirical designs are transparent and have been reanalysed and extended widely.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the China-shock work. Hanson is central to the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence. Katz has a long record on wage structure and the race between education and technology. Dorn and others were important co-authors on the China shock, and Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane and Goldin are adjacent contributors. The three-name limit makes the credit boundary imperfect.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from roughly 1998 to 2016. They have had years of replication, extension and critique, including debate over the size of the China shock and the role of automation.
uncertainties: Exact apportionment between Autor, Hanson, Katz and Dorn is debatable.
Some effect sizes are sensitive to specification and time period.
Overlap with recent prizes on technology and labour (Goldin, Acemoglu) may affect timing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work created a large empirical field linking legal institutions, investor protection and financial development. It shaped corporate governance, comparative finance and institutional economics, and it also bears on the institutions-and-prosperity agenda recognised in recent prizes. Its influence is large and has produced many follow-up papers.
assessment.attribution: La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny wrote the foundational papers together. Restricting to three requires omitting Vishny or Shleifer's other co-authors, and Shleifer's own wider work (behavioural finance, corporate finance) makes credit allocation awkward.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from the late 1990s and have had a long period of scrutiny.
uncertainties: Legal-origins identification and the causal interpretation have been criticised repeatedly (measurement of legal rules, endogeneity, colonial history).
Robustness of some cross-country regression results is debated.
Credit among four co-authors is difficult.
Reputational controversies around one nominee may matter for a committee.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work built long-run historical series on top incomes from tax records and reopened the study of income and wealth distribution. It shaped policy debate and research on taxation, and made inequality a mainstream empirical topic. Data construction and measurement are major contributions in themselves.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the clear originators of the top-income series, and Zucman is a later contributor on wealth and offshore holdings. Credit for the broader theory of capital and inequality is more contested than credit for the data.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work dates from the early 2000s and has been extended to many countries. The wealth and offshore work is more recent and less settled.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the wealth-concentration estimates and of tax-data assumptions.
The theoretical claims in the long-run capital narrative are disputed.
Whether the committee sees measurement and data as sufficient prize-level contributions.
Policy and political salience may complicate the assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference, such as double/debiased ML and causal forests, allow credible estimation of treatment effects with many covariates and heterogeneity. They are widely adopted in economics and neighbouring fields, and extend the credibility revolution recognised in 2021. They are useful to anyone concerned with reliable inference in large and noisy data.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov is central to double/debiased ML and high-dimensional inference. Athey and Wager (and Imbens) developed causal forests and related heterogeneous-effect methods. Athey also appears in other nominated areas. Credit overlaps with Imbens, Newey and others in semiparametric theory.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from about 2016 to 2018. Adoption has been rapid, but long-term validation is shorter than for the older candidates.
uncertainties: Whether the field is old enough for the committee to judge lasting impact.
Credit boundaries with semiparametric econometrics (Newey and others).
Practical performance in applications is mixed, and some replication evidence is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade theory changed the framing of trade, moving from industries to firms and showing selection and reallocation as channels for gains from trade. It is the basis of much modern empirical trade research, and the effects are visible in both data and policy analysis. The conceptual contribution is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the key model. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, and Redding, with others, extended it and estimated it. Krugman's earlier contributions are already recognised. Bernard, Eaton and Kortum are close contributors, which complicates the credit.
assessment.maturity: The model dates from 2003 and has had two decades of quantitative and empirical development.
uncertainties: Overlap with other nominated trade work (Helpman also appears elsewhere).
Parallel contributions by Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum.
Empirical magnitude of welfare gains depends on structural assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work gave a formal and experimentally grounded account of fairness and reciprocity, with models of inequity aversion and extensive experimental evidence on strong reciprocity and cooperation. It shaped contract theory, public economics and behavioural economics. The core experimental findings have been replicated widely, though effect sizes depend on context, which is a point I weigh as someone working with experimental replication. I apply the same criteria as for other fields despite that overlap in expertise.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr-Schmidt model and the experimental programme are strongly linked to Fehr, with Schmidt as co-author of the model and Falk as a notable empirical contributor. Bolton and Ockenfels (ERC model) are close parallel contributors who are not credited in this entry, and Rabin and Charness are adjacent.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 1999 and the early 2000s. There are many replications, field tests and extensions.
uncertainties: Parallel credit for Bolton and Ockenfels and for earlier fairness work.
Debate about how well lab social preferences generalise to field behaviour.
Behavioural economics has already been recognised through Kahneman, Thaler and Smith.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The weak-instrument literature showed that standard IV inference can be badly misleading, and produced identification-robust tests and practical diagnostics. It is directly relevant to the reliability of applied empirical work and complements the 2021 prize for causal inference with instruments. Applied researchers use the methods routinely.
assessment.attribution: Staiger and Stock (1997) is the key diagnostic paper. Andrews, with Moreira and Stock, developed the robust inference theory, and Yogo and Moreira contributed important tests and critical values. Bound, Jaeger and Baker, and Nelson and Startz, were early contributors. The three-name limit omits several important contributors.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s to the 2010s. It is well established and widely adopted.
uncertainties: Large and somewhat diffuse set of contributors.
Econometric-methods prizes are rarer and the committee may judge the contribution as technical or incremental relative to applied discoveries.
Overlap with other nominated econometrics entries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a tractable way to quantify how distortions across firms explain cross-country income and productivity differences. It had a large influence on growth, development and macroeconomics, and is a natural complement to the recent growth-focused prizes. It turned a qualitative idea into measurable magnitudes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) developed closely related ideas independently, which complicates attribution with a three-name limit that omits Rogerson.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2008 and 2009. There has been a long period of follow-up, but also continuing debate about measurement.
uncertainties: Measured misallocation is sensitive to measurement error, markup heterogeneity and adjustment costs.
Credit among Hsieh, Klenow, Restuccia and Rogerson.
The framework is largely accounting-based, so the committee may weigh its causal content differently.
